question: Why is a pound today worth more than a pound in three years' time?
model_answer_md:
For two reasons, and it is worth naming both.

First, **waiting has a cost**. If I had the pound now I could do something with it — repay a loan, open another shop, buy a gilt. Giving that up for three years means giving up whatever I would have earned, which economists call the opportunity cost.

Second, **the future pound might not arrive**. The payer could go bust or dispute the invoice; the promise is not the cash.

The discount rate prices both together. It is the return I could earn elsewhere on something of similar risk, so dividing by it converts a future amount into what I would need today to be indifferent between the two.
key_points: Opportunity cost — the pound could be invested or used now
Risk — a future payment may not arrive in full or at all
The discount rate prices both, set by returns available elsewhere at similar risk
Discounting is the reverse of compounding, not an inflation adjustment

follow_ups.question: Isn't this just inflation?
follow_ups.answer_md: Inflation is one component but not the main one. In a world with zero inflation you would still prefer the pound now, because you could invest it and because the future payment carries risk. Inflation matters mostly for consistency: discount nominal cash flows at a nominal rate, and real cash flows at a real rate — mixing the two is the actual mistake.

follow_ups.question: Which cash flows get the highest discount rate?
follow_ups.answer_md: The riskiest and least certain ones. A government bond coupon is discounted at close to the risk-free rate; an equity stake in an early-stage, cash-burning business is discounted at a much higher rate, because the range of outcomes is far wider and shareholders are paid last.

weak_answer_note: Says only 'because of inflation', or asserts that money 'loses value over time' without naming opportunity cost or risk. A weak answer also treats it as a rule to recite rather than explaining why a rate is applied at all.
